fields.oneLiner: ReelStock keeps a saree reseller's stock count straight across Instagram, so a piece already sold in a DM stops being promised to two more people.
fields.jobStory:
When a saree reseller posts a reel at 9pm and forty DMs come in overnight for eleven pieces she actually has, she wants the stock to be marked the moment a piece is confirmed, so I can stop refunding two customers a week and apologising for a saree she sold twice.

Who has this job: Instagram-first saree resellers in Surat and Rajkot with between 4,000 and 60,000 followers, who buy in small lots from the Surat textile market and sell one or two pieces at a time through reels and DMs. Nearly all of them are women running it alone or with one helper, and you can find hundreds of them just from the hashtags under any Surat wholesale reel. I interviewed twelve, eight of them over video call.

What they do instead: a notebook and their own memory, or a Google Sheet on a phone that they update between replies. Nine of the twelve had double-sold a piece in the last month, and six said they simply stop replying to DMs when a reel goes well, because replying is what causes the mistake. One had moved to marking pieces sold by editing the caption, which works until the reel gets reposted.
fields.trafficTestNotes:
One big source and one small one, 2 to 12 September 2026.

1. A giveaway collab with two saree reseller pages, 38k and 74k followers. The post said: follow both pages, and sign up on the link to enter a draw for a 2,000 rupee saree and a free year of ReelStock when it launches. I paid 2,000 for the saree and 1,500 to one of the two pages, the other did it for free. Instagram insights across both posts: 118,000 accounts reached, 3,880 link taps. 1,240 of those landed on my page according to the short link, and 197 signed up.

2. A WhatsApp group of Surat market suppliers, about 120 members, one post on 11 Sep. 22 clicks, 13 signups, free.

Total spend 3,500 rupees, 1,262 visits, 210 signups, 16.6%. I know the giveaway inflates this. Some of these emails are people who want a free saree and have never sold anything. When I launch I will treat the 13 from the supplier group as the real ones and everything from the giveaway as a maybe.

notes: Borderline, and a human could argue it either way. The traffic write-up is honest about the giveaway skewing the number, which is why traffic-test survives. It returns on evidence: the screenshot is a spreadsheet the student maintains himself rather than the tool that collected the emails, and it shows 214 rows against a reported 210, so nothing in it can be checked. A generous reviewer would call the four-row gap a rounding artefact and pass.
